title: Convergence theorems, uniform integrability, and densities

sections.title: Shrinking supports with freely growing heights
paragraphs: Continue the shrinking-spike example on the uniform interval: $$X_n(\omega)=a_n\mathbf1_{(0,1/n]}(\omega),\qquad a_n\ge0.$$ For every fixed $\omega>0$, $X_n(\omega)=0$ eventually, so $X_n\to X_\infty=0$ almost surely. Its mean is $$\mathbb E X_n=\frac{a_n}{n}.$$ Choosing $a_n/n\to\infty$ makes the means diverge even though the variables converge almost surely to zero. In particular, there is no convergence in $L^1$.
editorial: More generally, $\mathbb E|X_n|^p=a_n^p/n$. The support probability, the height, and their product play different roles: vanishing support can ensure probability convergence while tall values prevent moment convergence.

sections.title: Monotone convergence and Fatou lower envelopes
paragraphs: Monotone convergence in probability notation: if $X_n\ge0$ and $X_n\uparrow X_\infty$ almost surely, then $$\mathbb E X_n\uparrow\mathbb E X_\infty.$$ If $\mathbb E X_\infty<\infty$, then also $X_n\to X_\infty$ in $L^1$, since $\mathbb E|X_\infty-X_n|=\mathbb E X_\infty-\mathbb E X_n\to0$.
Fatou lemma: if $X_n\ge Y$ almost surely for every $n$, with $\mathbb E|Y|<\infty$, then $$\liminf_n\mathbb E X_n\ge\mathbb E(\liminf_n X_n).$$
proof: Set $$Z_n=\inf_{m\ge n}X_m.$$ These are measurable, $Z_n\uparrow\liminf_nX_n$, and $Z_n\ge Y$ outside one common null event. Apply monotone convergence to the nonnegative sequence $Z_n-Y$ to obtain $$\lim_n\mathbb E Z_n=\mathbb E(\liminf_nX_n).$$

For every $m\ge n$, $X_m\ge Z_n$, hence $\mathbb E X_m\ge\mathbb E Z_n$. Take the infimum over $m\ge n$ and then let $n\to\infty$ to get $$\liminf_n\mathbb E X_n\ge\lim_n\mathbb E Z_n=\mathbb E(\liminf_nX_n).$$ The lecture describes monotone convergence as Fatou for an increasing sequence.
editorial: All almost-sure inequalities can be arranged on one event of probability one because the sequence is countable. An integrable lower bound makes the signed expectations well-defined and permits subtracting $\mathbb E Y$. Applying Fatou to $-X_n$ similarly gives a reverse limsup inequality when the sequence has an integrable upper bound.

recall.question: How does the tail infimum turn Fatou into an application of monotone convergence?
answer: Take $Z_n=\inf_{m\ge n}X_m$. Then $Z_n$ increases to the pointwise liminf. Subtract the common integrable lower bound $Y$ to apply monotone convergence. Since $Z_n\le X_m$ for every $m\ge n$, its expectation is bounded by the corresponding tail infimum of expectations.
checks: Use the whole tail, not a finite preview.
Take an infimum before the final limit.

sections.title: Dominated convergence, bounded convergence, and Scheffé
paragraphs: Dominated convergence: suppose $X_n\to X_\infty$ almost surely and $|X_n|\le Y$ almost surely for all $n$, where $\mathbb E Y<\infty$. Then $X_\infty$ is integrable and $$\mathbb E|X_n-X_\infty|\longrightarrow0.$$ In particular, $\mathbb E X_n\to\mathbb E X_\infty$.
Bounded convergence is the special case $|X_n|\le C<\infty$ for one nonrandom constant $C$. Almost-sure convergence then implies convergence in $L^1$.
Scheffé lemma: suppose $X_n,X_\infty\in L^1$ for every $n$, $X_n\to X_\infty$ almost surely, and $$\mathbb E|X_n|\longrightarrow\mathbb E|X_\infty|<\infty.$$ Then $X_n\to X_\infty$ in $L^1$.
proof: For dominated convergence, take the limit in $|X_n|\le Y$ to get $|X_\infty|\le Y$, so $\mathbb E|X_\infty|\le\mathbb E Y<\infty$. The errors satisfy $|X_n-X_\infty|\le2Y$. Fatou applied to $2Y-|X_n-X_\infty|\ge0$ gives $$\limsup_n\mathbb E|X_n-X_\infty|\le\mathbb E(\limsup_n|X_n-X_\infty|)=0.$$ Nonnegativity finishes the proof.
editorial: The handwritten pages state Scheffé without a proof. Retain integrability of every term and the finite limiting absolute moment; equality of signed means alone does not replace these conditions. Convergence of absolute integrals to a finite value guarantees integrability only eventually, so any earlier nonintegrable terms must be discarded before using the definition of an $L^1$-convergent sequence. The dominated-convergence proof uses the factor $2$ because both the approximant and its limit are bounded by $Y$. Bounded convergence here uses a probability space; on an infinite-measure space a constant roof need not be integrable.

sections.title: Uniform integrability, small events, and Vitali
paragraphs: A family $\{X_\alpha:\alpha\in I\}$ is uniformly integrable if $$\lim_{M\to\infty}\sup_{\alpha\in I}\mathbb E\bigl[|X_\alpha|\mathbf1_{\{|X_\alpha|>M\}}\bigr]=0.$$ Equivalently, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is one finite $M$ such that the displayed tail expectation is less than $\varepsilon$ for every $\alpha$.

Every uniformly integrable family satisfies the following small-event consequence: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that for every $\alpha\in I$ and $A\in\mathcal F$ with $\mathbb P(A)<\delta$, $$\mathbb E[|X_\alpha|\mathbf1_A]<\varepsilon.$$

An integrable common roof is sufficient for uniform integrability: if $|X_n|\le Y$ almost surely and $\mathbb E Y<\infty$, then $$\sup_n\mathbb E\bigl[|X_n|\mathbf1_{\{|X_n|>M\}}\bigr]\le\mathbb E[Y\mathbf1_{\{Y>M\}}]\longrightarrow0.$$ The final limit follows from monotone convergence applied to $Y\mathbf1_{\{Y\le M\}}\uparrow Y$, or from dominated convergence.
editorial: The small-event line on p49 is shorthand and does not visibly carry all absolute-value bars or hypotheses. The uniform-integrability consequence requires the absolute integral as displayed. Indeed, split $\mathbb E[|X_\alpha|\mathbf1_A]\le M\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb E[|X_\alpha|\mathbf1_{\{|X_\alpha|>M\}}]$ and choose $M$, then $\delta$.

For an equivalence on an arbitrary probability space, add uniform $L^1$ boundedness: a family is uniformly integrable if and only if $\sup_\alpha\mathbb E|X_\alpha|<\infty$ and the small-event condition holds. For the reverse direction, Markov makes $\mathbb P(|X_\alpha|>M)\le C/M$ uniformly small. The small-event condition alone is insufficient on a one-point probability space: constants $X_n=n$ satisfy it vacuously for $\delta<1$ but are not uniformly integrable.

Vitali is stated on the handwritten page without its general proof. Under convergence in probability, it is also equivalent to integrability of every $X_n$ and $X_\infty$ together with $\mathbb E|X_n|\to\mathbb E|X_\infty|$. Uniform integrability also implies uniform $L^1$ boundedness by $\mathbb E|X_\alpha|\le M+\sup_\beta\mathbb E[|X_\beta|\mathbf1_{\{|X_\beta|>M\}}]$.

recall.question: What extra condition upgrades convergence in probability to convergence in L1? How does domination imply it?
answer: Vitali requires uniform integrability: all members have small absolute tail expectations beyond one common large cutoff. If $|X_n|\le Y\in L^1$, each tail is bounded by $Y\mathbf1_{\{Y>M\}}$, whose expectation tends to zero. Uniform integrability controls expected mass, while an $L^1$ bound alone does not.
checks: The cutoff must be uniform over the family.
Convergence in probability is still required.
Small-event control alone needs a separate uniform L1 bound for the converse.

sections.title: A CDF determines a unique probability measure
paragraphs: If $F:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ is nondecreasing and right-continuous, with $F(-\infty)=0$ and $F(+\infty)=1$ in the limiting sense, then there is a unique probability measure $\nu$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B_{\mathbb R})$ such that $$\nu(( -\infty,t])=F(t)\quad\text{for every }t\in\mathbb R.$$
editorial: This restates the earlier CDF theorem in measure language. Existence follows, for example, from the quantile construction; uniqueness follows from the generating half-line $\pi$-system. Neither direction is proved again on this page.

sections.title: A nonnegative function defines a weighted measure
paragraphs:
If $f:\mathbb R	o[0,\infty]$ is Borel measurable, it defines a measure $
u=f\lambda$ on the real line by $$
u(A)=\int_A f(x)\,dx.$$ In particular, whenever $F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}f(t)\,dt$ is finite, $
u((a,b])=F(b)-F(a)=\int_{(a,b]}f(x)\,dx$.

More generally, fix $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mu)$ and a nonnegative measurable $f$. Define $$f_\mu=f\mu,\qquad f_\mu(A)=\mu(f\mathbf1_A),\quad A\in\mathcal F.$$ Then $f_\mu$ is a measure. The lecture states the composition rule $$h(f\mu)=(hf)\mu\quad(f,h\ge0\text{ measurable}),$$ and the integration identity $$h\in L^1(\Omega,\mathcal F,f\mu)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad fh\in L^1(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mu),\qquad \int h\,d(f\mu)=\int hf\,d\mu.$$
proof: Nonnegativity and $f_\mu(\varnothing)=0$ follow from the definition. If $A_k$ are disjoint measurable sets, monotone convergence gives $$f_\mu\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty}A_k\right)=\mu\left(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}f\mathbf1_{A_k}\right)=\lim_n\mu\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}f\mathbf1_{A_k}\right)=\lim_n\sum_{k=1}^{n}f_\mu(A_k)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}f_\mu(A_k).$$ Thus $f_\mu$ is countably additive.
editorial: The lecture writes both $f_\mu$ and $f\mu$ for the same measure. For arbitrary nonnegative $f$, the measure is defined directly by integrating $f\mathbf1_A$; a finite CDF antiderivative is unnecessary. Products of nonnegative extended values use $0\cdot\infty=0$.

sections.title: The standard machine for composition and change of measure
paragraphs: To prove $h(f\mu)=(hf)\mu$, fix $A\in\mathcal F$ and prove $$(f\mu)(h\mathbf1_A)=\mu(fh\mathbf1_A).$$ The notes organize the proof as indicators, simple functions, increasing approximation, then the signed split.
proof: For a nonnegative simple function $h=\sum_{i=1}^{m}c_i\mathbf1_{B_i}$, linearity and the indicator case give $$h(f\mu)(A)=\sum_i c_i(f\mu)(A\cap B_i)=\sum_i c_i\mu(f\mathbf1_{A\cap B_i})=\mu(fh\mathbf1_A).$$

For general $h\ge0$, choose nonnegative simple $h_n\uparrow h$. Monotone convergence first under $f\mu$ and then under $\mu$ gives $$h(f\mu)(A)=\lim_n(f\mu)(h_n\mathbf1_A)=\lim_n\mu(fh_n\mathbf1_A)=\mu(fh\mathbf1_A)=((hf)\mu)(A).$$ This proves equality of measures.

Set $A=\Omega$ to deduce for $h\ge0$ that $$(f\mu)(h)=(f\mu)(h\mathbf1_\Omega)=h(f\mu)(\Omega)=((hf)\mu)(\Omega)=\mu(fh).$$ For signed $h=h_+-h_-$, apply the nonnegative identity to each part. Applying it first to $|h|$ proves that $h$ is integrable for $f\mu$ exactly when $fh$ is integrable for $\mu$; then subtract the two finite signed parts.
editorial: The last integrability check must precede signed subtraction. The monotone-convergence step is used in both measure spaces, and relies on $f\ge0$ so $fh_n\mathbf1_A\uparrow fh\mathbf1_A$.

recall.question: Prove $\int h\,d(f\mu)=\int hf\,d\mu$ using the four stages of the standard machine.
answer: For an indicator, both sides are $\mu(f\mathbf1_B)$. Linearity extends the identity to nonnegative simple functions. Approximate an arbitrary nonnegative $h$ increasingly by simple functions and use monotone convergence under both measures. Apply the nonnegative identity to $|h|$ to verify integrability, then subtract the positive and negative identities for signed $h$.
checks: Use monotone convergence on both sides.

sections.title: Densities, absolute continuity, and Radon–Nikodym
paragraphs:
If measures $\mu,
u$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ satisfy $\mu=f
u$ for a nonnegative measurable $f$, say that $\mu$ has density $f$ with respect to $
u$. Then $$
u(A)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mu(A)=0\qquad(A\in\mathcal F).$$ This property is called absolute continuity and is written $\mu\ll
u$.

Radon–Nikodym theorem: if $\mu$ and $
u$ are both $\sigma$-finite measures on $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ and $\mu\ll
u$, then there exists a nonnegative measurable $f$ such that $$\mu=f
u.$$ The density is denoted $$ rac{d\mu}{d
u}=f.$$
proof:
The implication from a density to absolute continuity is immediate: if $
u(A)=0$, then $f\mathbf1_A=0$ $
u$-almost everywhere, so $$\mu(A)=\int f\mathbf1_A\,d
u=0.$$
editorial: The notes state Radon–Nikodym but do not prove its converse/existence assertion. Both $\sigma$-finiteness hypotheses are visible and are retained. A finite-valued version of the density can be chosen, and it is unique up to $\nu$-almost-everywhere equality. This theorem is Dembo 4.1.5, not an entry currently present in the Chapters 1–2 companion; its early appearance is part of the lecture order.

sections.title: Density examples, a Dirac obstruction, and restriction
paragraphs: If $\nu=\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$ and $\mu=f\lambda$ is a probability measure, then its distribution function is $$F_\mu(x)=\mu(( -\infty,x])=\int_{-\infty}^{x}f(t)\,dt.$$ Thus an ordinary probability density is a Radon–Nikodym density with respect to Lebesgue measure.

For a fixed $x\in\mathbb R$, the Dirac measure is $$\delta_x(A)=\begin{cases}1,&x\in A,\\0,&x\notin A.\end{cases}$$ It is not absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure: choose $A=\{x\}$, for which $\lambda(A)=0$ but $\delta_x(A)=1$. Hence it has no Lebesgue density.

For a measure space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mu)$ and $D\in\mathcal F$, the restricted measurable space and measure are $$(D,\mathcal F_D,\mu_D),\qquad \mathcal F_D=\{A\cap D:A\in\mathcal F\},\qquad \mu_D=\mu|_{\mathcal F_D}.$$ The weighted measure $\mathbf1_D\mu$ on $\Omega$ agrees with $\mu_D$ on subsets of $D$. For nonnegative measurable $h$ on $\Omega$, $$\int_D h\,d\mu_D=\int_\Omega h\mathbf1_D\,d\mu.$$
editorial: The diagram shows $D$ sitting inside $\Omega$. Restriction preserves the original mass $\mu(D)$; the lecture does not normalize it to a conditional probability. The notation $\mu_D=\mathbf1_D\mu$ is read with its domains understood: $\mu_D$ lives on $D$, while the weighted measure lives on $\Omega$. The same integration formula holds for a signed $h$ whenever $h\mathbf1_D$ is integrable.
